rapacious

ruh-PAY-shuhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Rapacious is aggressively greedy or grasping, especially for money or power.

Historians describe the empire's rapacious taxation of conquered provinces as one of the chief causes of its eventual collapse.

Example

Local fishermen accused the new corporation of rapacious overfishing, hauling in every last catch without regard for next season's supply.

The company wasn't just profitable -- it was grasping for as much as possible with no restraint, which is the aggressive greed at the heart of rapacious.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

greedy: Greedy is the broad, everyday word for wanting more of something than you need -- food, money, toys, attention. Rapacious sharpens and darkens it: aggressive greed on the scale of plunder, almost always for money or power.

grasping: Grasping paints greed you can almost see -- hands closing around money, a person forever scheming to get a little more of it. It is ugly but personal and small-scale. Rapacious blows the picture up: aggressive, plundering greed for money or power, seizing on a grand scale.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

generous: willing to give more than is strictly necessary

content: satisfied with what one already has

Where it sits · how aggressively it grabs for gain — acquisitive → rapacious → predatory

acquisitive vs. rapacious: Acquisitive is weaker than rapacious: an acquisitive collector simply loves gaining new things, while rapacious greed grabs at money or power with aggressive, grasping force.

predatory vs. rapacious: Predatory is stronger than rapacious: rapacious greed grabs whatever it can, but a predatory schemer goes further, actively hunting and exploiting victims for gain.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — rapac

Root — rapac: to seize, snatch, or carry off swiftly (from Latin rapere, 'to seize'; rapax, rapacis means 'grasping')

Suffix — -ious

Suffix — -ious: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Rapacious combines rapac ('grasping,' from Latin rapere, 'to seize or snatch') with -ious -- the same ancient root that gives English the word rapid. Something rapacious seizes and grabs at every opportunity, aggressively and without restraint.

Use the root in a new word: rapid

Use the root in a new word: rapid: The rapid current swept the canoe downstream before anyone could react.

Root Check

Word Choice

Rapacious is a strong word -- reserve it for aggressive, almost predatory greed, not ordinary ambition or thrift. Fun fact: this unit's own rapturous comes from that same ancient root, rapere, 'to seize' -- one word seizes greedily, the other feels swept away, or seized, by joy.
